declared.title: Early-career setback and future career impact
declared.foundIn: Crossref search « early-career setback and future career impact near miss » (2026-11-23)

population: 561 narrow winners and 623 near misses among junior applicants for NIH R01 grants (USA, 1990-2005), proposals just above or below the funding threshold

findings.text: A near miss made junior scientists more likely to leave for good: more than a 10% higher chance of disappearing from the NIH system (12.6% over ten years, full text)

support.sentence: On the one hand, it significantly increases attrition, predicting more than a 10% chance of disappearing permanently from the NIH system.

findings.text: Among those who stayed active, near misses later published more highly cited work than narrow winners (measured after the setback had pushed others out)

support.sentence: Yet, despite an early setback, individuals with near misses systematically outperform those with narrow wins in the longer run.

findings.text: The authors argue the advantage is not only that the weaker left: the setback « seems » to cause an improvement in those who persevere

support.sentence: Moreover, this performance advantage seems to go beyond a screening mechanism, suggesting early-career setback appears to cause a performance improvement among those who persevere.

limits: quasi-experiment (fuzzy regression discontinuity at the funding cut-off): causal for leaving, not for performance
performance is compared « conditional on remaining active in the NIH system » (full text), after a selection the setback itself causes
small gain: after matching, citations 30.8 vs 27.7, Cohen's d = 0.05 (full text)
Traag et al. 2025 (eLife reviewed preprint, 14 programmes, 6 funders): the setback effect « is not robust » and is likely a selection effect
the authors: their results « do not imply that one should strategically put roadblocks in the way of junior scientists »
one select group (US biomedical scientists); outcome = later publications and citations, not learning
